name: GlobeNet

profile.address: 376, East Main Street, Tuckerton Meadows, Paradise Cove, Tuckerton, Ocean County, New Jersey, 08087
profile.reading:
The GlobeNet Tuckerton Cable Landing Station, at 376 East Main Street in Tuckerton, New Jersey, is a submarine fiber-optic cable landing facility rather than a conventional colocation or cloud data center. It is one of two landing stations in Tuckerton -- AT&T operates a separate, unrelated facility nearby for the transatlantic TAT-14 cable system -- and it serves as the U.S. terminus for the GlobeNet cable network, a roughly 23,500-kilometer subsea system linking the U.S. East Coast to Bermuda, Brazil, Colombia and Venezuela.

The cable system dates to 2001, when it was built and launched by 360 Networks, a fiber carrier that filed for bankruptcy protection the same year construction wrapped. Brasil Telecom acquired the system out of that restructuring in 2003 for roughly $46.8 million and renamed it GlobeNet. Brasil Telecom's 2009 merger with Telemar formed Oi S.A., which held the cable through the following decade. In 2013, Oi sold its submarine-cable subsidiary to investment group BTG Pactual for about $768 million, and the Tuckerton facility has operated under BTG-affiliated ownership since. Between 2021 and 2022, BTG Pactual took a controlling stake in V.tal, the fiber-infrastructure spinoff of Oi, and in September 2022 completed a merger folding GlobeNet fully into V.tal -- so the Tuckerton station is today part of V.tal's Latin American wholesale telecom portfolio, still branded and filed with U.S. regulators under the GlobeNet name.

The station's most significant technical expansion came in April 2013, when GlobeNet completed a new Bermuda-to-Tuckerton cable segment (Segment 5) using TE SubCom submarine line terminating equipment, delivering roughly 30 terabits per second of design capacity across 150 wavelengths per fiber pair at 100 Gbps each -- at the time, GlobeNet described it as having the largest cross-sectional capacity per fiber pair of any system built or under contract. Regulatory filings with the FCC show the Tuckerton facility anchors two of GlobeNet's licensed cable segments: Tuckerton-to-Boca Raton, Florida (about 1,820 km) and St. David's, Bermuda-to-Tuckerton (about 1,370 km). GlobeNet's original 25-year landing license dates to 1999 and was set to expire in March 2026; a renewal application filed in July 2025 seeks a new license running through March 2051, indicating the operator intends to keep the station in long-term service.

As a carrier cable landing facility rather than a marketed data hall, GlobeNet does not publish building square footage, power capacity, or industry certifications for the Tuckerton site -- routine disclosures for retail colocation providers, but not standard practice for landing stations, which primarily house submarine line terminating equipment and connect to inland fiber backhaul rather than lease space to tenants.

reading.body:
GlobeNet operates a 26,000-kilometer subsea cable network connecting the Americas, with its US presence anchored to two cable landing stations rather than commercial data center capacity.

GlobeNet's infrastructure strategy differs fundamentally from the colocation and hyperscale operators dominating this registry. The Tuckerton, New Jersey facility functions as a cable landing point and network presence, not a standalone colocation product. Its purpose is to terminate subsea fiber and interconnect US carriers and content providers to GlobeNet's broader Latin American network, a role distinct from buildings designed for tenant compute density.

The company's recent expansion into data centers, interconnection points, and security services in Colombia, Brazil, and Argentina suggests a gradual shift toward offering services beyond pure transport. However, the data does not cover power capacity, building footprint, or compute hosting specifications for any GlobeNet facility. The Tuckerton station's historical context, built on Cold War-era underground infrastructure originally supporting now-decommissioned transatlantic cables, indicates repurposed rather than purpose-built capacity for current needs.

For the thesis that grid constraint binds AI scaling, GlobeNet represents the inverse problem: a network operator with established connectivity between continents and growing data center footprint in Latin America, but no published power consumption or capacity figures. This leaves the question open whether regional data center expansion is compute-limited by available grid capacity or by other factors.
